The two data sets aggregate to form more robust results than either alone. However, even when combined, CE-CERT and FleetDNA data are not robust for all source types, types of roads, and days over all hours, so we give specific recommendations on which data to consider using for incorporating into MOVES. On freeways, vehicles spend most of their time at 50–65 miles per hour (mph) per each source type. On other roads, vehicles tend to travel much slower, often spending the most time in the 5– 10-mph bin. Aside from combination-unit long-haul trucks, most FleetDNA and CE-CERT data point to slower average speeds than the current MOVES defaults show. In particular, this data set has slower average speeds for transit buses, school buses, and refuse trucks, which is expected due to their stop-and-go duty cycles. In general, we did not observe meaningful differences in average speed across hours of the day. For use in MOVES, we recommend using average speed distributions calculated by source type, road type, and day type (weekday or weekend). For VMT road type distributions, we compare road type distributions to MOVES defaults. Long- haul combination truck road type distributions compare well to the current MOVES defaults. The remaining source types have road type distributions with more driving on urban roads than the MOVES defaults. The road type distributions developed in this study may be used to represent local urban fleets and update the relative proportions on urban freeways compared to urban other roads, but we do not recommend editing the rural-to-urban ratio of the MOVES defaults based on primarily urban fleet data. For VMT day distributions, we observe that many of the source types have significantly different weekday vs. weekend splits in driving behavior. We see that combination-unit long-haul vehicles tend to drive more on weekends, whereas refuse trucks and school buses drive more on weekdays than predicted by MOVES. We recommend that the day type distribution for several source types from MOVES be updated. For VMT hour distributions, weekdays often do not show the two peaks characteristic of MOVES defaults and tend to drive more miles in the morning hours relative to MOVES defaults.
